about: Organisation of the Body is one of the subjects of the First BM Part I at Oxford, studied by first-year medical students across the year. It is the anatomy-led strand of the integrated First BM syllabus, running from cells, microscopy and the basic tissues through the peripheral nervous system, limb and spinal anatomy, and each body system, to embryology and blood. It is examined in two parts: Part A, a computer-based paper testing breadth across the core syllabus, and Part B, testing deeper knowledge of selected topics from the core and extension syllabus. The Medical Sciences syllabus says subjects 1–3 have MCQ and essay components, with a choice of essay questions.
topics: Cell structure, organelles and the cell cycle
Cell growth, differentiation and abnormal growth
Peripheral nervous system tissues, divisions and muscle innervation
Musculoskeletal anatomy: limbs, joints, spine, imaging
Abdomen, GI tract, liver and pancreas
Blood: haematopoiesis, blood cells and haemostasis

notes.h: Cell structure, organelles and the cell cycle
notes.body:
Organisation of the Body begins with the cell, because every tissue and organ you meet later is built from cells whose structure explains their function. You should be able to describe each organelle, give an example of a cell type in which it is prominent, and link it to a disease.

The plasma membrane
- A phospholipid bilayer with cholesterol and integral and peripheral proteins (the fluid mosaic model of Singer and Nicolson, 1972).
- Carbohydrate chains on the outer surface form the glycocalyx, involved in recognition and adhesion.

Nucleus
- Bounded by a double-membrane nuclear envelope that is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum and perforated by nuclear pores.
- Chromatin is either euchromatin (loosely packed, transcriptionally active, pale) or heterochromatin (condensed, inactive, dark).
- The nucleolus is where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled; it is large in cells making lots of protein.

The secretory and endocytic pathways
- Rough ER: ribosome-studded; makes proteins destined for secretion, membranes or lysosomes. Abundant in plasma cells and pancreatic acinar cells, giving basophilic cytoplasm.
- Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis (adrenal cortex, Leydig cells), detoxification (hepatocytes) and calcium storage (the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle).
- Golgi apparatus: receives vesicles at its cis face, modifies proteins (for example glycosylation) and sorts them at the trans face. Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate; failure of this tagging causes I-cell disease.
- Exocytosis may be constitutive (continuous) or regulated (stored granules released on a signal, for example insulin from beta cells).
- Endocytosis includes clathrin-mediated uptake of specific ligands, such as LDL by the LDL receptor.

Other organelles
- Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases working at about pH 5. Missing enzymes cause lysosomal storage diseases, for example Tay–Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A).
- Mitochondria have a double membrane with cristae, their own circular DNA (inherited maternally) and carry out oxidative phosphorylation. Release of cytochrome c triggers intrinsic apoptosis. They are plentiful in cardiac muscle and renal proximal tubule cells.
- Peroxisomes contain catalase and oxidise very long chain fatty acids.

Cytoskeleton
- Actin microfilaments (about 7 nm): cell shape, microvilli cores, muscle contraction.
- Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm): tensile strength; tissue-specific types such as keratins (epithelia), vimentin (mesenchymal cells), desmin (muscle), neurofilaments and nuclear lamins. Useful in pathology to identify a tumour's tissue of origin.
- Microtubules (about 25 nm): tubulin polymers organised from the centrosome; tracks for kinesin (towards the plus end, usually outward) and dynein (towards the minus end); form the mitotic spindle and the 9+2 axoneme of cilia.

The cell cycle
- Phases: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation), M (mitosis and cytokinesis). Non-dividing cells sit in G0.
- Progression is driven by cyclins binding cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).
- Checkpoints: G1/S (the restriction point, controlled by Rb and p53), G2/M (DNA damage), and the spindle assembly checkpoint at metaphase–anaphase.
- Mitosis: prophase (chromosomes condense), prometaphase (nuclear envelope breaks down, kinetochores attach), metaphase (alignment), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase (envelopes reform), then cytokinesis by an actin–myosin contractile ring.
- A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes; after S phase each consists of two sister chromatids.

Clinical link: several anticancer drugs act on microtubules (vinca alkaloids prevent assembly, taxanes stabilise them), arresting cells in mitosis.

Exam tips: in the MCQ, expect organelle–function and organelle–cell type pairings; in essays, structure each answer as structure, function, example cell, clinical relevance.

notes.h: Normal control of growth and differentiation; abnormalities of growth
notes.body:
Tissues stay a constant size because cell production balances cell loss. This topic links the cell cycle to tissue biology and to the basic language of pathology.

Cell populations by capacity to divide
- Labile cells divide continuously throughout life: epidermis, gut epithelium, bone marrow.
- Stable (quiescent) cells normally sit in G0 but can re-enter the cycle when needed: hepatocytes, renal tubular cells, fibroblasts.
- Permanent cells cannot divide in adults: most neurons and cardiac myocytes. Skeletal muscle repairs only through satellite cells.

Stem cells
- Defined by self-renewal plus the ability to give rise to differentiated cells.
- Potency: totipotent (zygote, can form embryo and placenta), pluripotent (inner cell mass, embryonic stem cells), multipotent (haematopoietic stem cells), unipotent.
- Adult stem cells live in niches, for example the base of intestinal crypts, the basal layer of the epidermis and the hair follicle bulge.
- Asymmetric division produces one stem cell and one committed progenitor (transit-amplifying cell).

Control of proliferation and differentiation
- Growth factors (for example EGF, PDGF) act on receptor tyrosine kinases and the Ras–MAPK pathway to drive cells from G0 into G1.
- Contact inhibition and anti-growth signals restrain division.
- Differentiation results from differential gene expression controlled by transcription factors; terminally differentiated cells, such as surface keratinocytes, do not divide.
- Apoptosis removes unwanted cells: an energy-dependent, caspase-driven programme with cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, fragmentation into apoptotic bodies and phagocytosis without inflammation. It may be intrinsic (mitochondrial, regulated by the BCL-2 family, cytochrome c release) or extrinsic (death receptors such as Fas).
- Necrosis, by contrast, is uncontrolled death with swelling, membrane rupture and inflammation.

Adaptive changes
- Hypertrophy: increase in cell size (skeletal muscle with training; left ventricle in hypertension). The only option for permanent cells.
- Hyperplasia: increase in cell number (endometrium in the proliferative phase; benign prostatic hyperplasia).
- Atrophy: decrease in size or number (disuse, denervation, reduced blood supply).
- Metaplasia: reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another, usually as a response to chronic irritation. Examples: bronchial pseudostratified ciliated epithelium becoming stratified squamous in smokers; oesophageal squamous epithelium becoming glandular (columnar) in Barrett's oesophagus due to acid reflux.

Dysplasia and neoplasia
- Dysplasia: disordered growth with nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism, increased mitoses and loss of maturation; a pre-malignant change that has not breached the basement membrane.
- Neoplasia: an abnormal mass whose growth is excessive, uncoordinated with normal tissue and persists after the original stimulus is removed.
- Benign tumours are usually well differentiated, slow-growing, encapsulated and do not invade. Malignant tumours invade and can metastasise via lymphatics, blood or across body cavities.
- Naming: epithelial malignancy = carcinoma (adenocarcinoma if glandular); mesenchymal malignancy = sarcoma; benign tumours usually end in -oma (adenoma, lipoma).
- Genetic basis: activation of oncogenes (gain of function, often dominant, for example RAS) and loss of tumour suppressor genes (both copies, for example RB1 and TP53, Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, 1971).
- Hanahan and Weinberg's "hallmarks of cancer" (2000, updated 2011) include sustained proliferative signalling, evading growth suppressors, resisting cell death, replicative immortality (telomerase), angiogenesis, and invasion and metastasis.

Exam tips: define each adaptive change precisely and give a named tissue example; essays on growth control score well when they link molecular control (cyclins, Rb, p53) to tissue-level outcomes.

Much of Organisation of the Body is learned through histology, so you need to understand how images are produced and what their limits are. Questions often ask why a structure looks the way it does in a given preparation.

Resolution
- Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as separate. It depends on wavelength and numerical aperture (NA): d ≈ λ / (2 NA).
- With visible light (λ about 500 nm) and an oil-immersion objective (NA about 1.4), d is about 0.2 µm. This is why light microscopy shows cells and nuclei but not ribosomes or membranes in detail.
- Magnification without extra resolution ("empty magnification") reveals no new detail.

Preparing tissue for light microscopy
- Fixation (commonly formalin) cross-links proteins to preserve structure and stop autolysis.
- Dehydration in graded alcohols, clearing (for example xylene), embedding in paraffin wax.
- Sectioning on a microtome, typically a few micrometres thick, then mounting and staining.
- Frozen sections are quicker (used during operations) and keep lipids, which are dissolved out in routine processing; that is why adipocytes look empty in H&E sections.

Stains
- Haematoxylin is basic and stains acidic (basophilic) structures blue-purple: nuclei (DNA) and RNA-rich cytoplasm with lots of rough ER.
- Eosin is acidic and stains basic (eosinophilic/acidophilic) structures pink: most cytoplasmic proteins, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, collagen.
- Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains carbohydrate-rich material magenta: glycogen, mucins, basement membranes, brush borders.
- Other special stains: trichrome stains for collagen, silver stains for reticular fibres, Oil red O or Sudan stains for lipid on frozen sections.
- Immunohistochemistry uses labelled antibodies to locate a specific protein.

Other light techniques
- Phase contrast and differential interference contrast turn differences in refractive index into contrast, allowing unstained living cells to be viewed.
- Fluorescence microscopy: a fluorophore absorbs light of one wavelength and emits light of a longer wavelength (the Stokes shift); filters separate them. Labels include fluorescent antibodies (direct or indirect immunofluorescence), DNA dyes and genetically encoded proteins such as GFP for live imaging.
- Confocal microscopy uses a pinhole to reject out-of-focus light, giving thin optical sections that can be stacked into 3D reconstructions.
- Super-resolution methods get round the diffraction limit by special illumination or single-molecule localisation.

Electron microscopy
- Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so resolution for biological specimens is around a nanometre or better, showing membranes, ribosomes and the cytoskeleton.
- Transmission EM (TEM): fixation with glutaraldehyde then osmium tetroxide (which stabilises and stains lipids), resin embedding, ultrathin sections (tens of nanometres), contrast from heavy metals such as uranyl acetate and lead citrate. Dense regions scatter electrons and look dark (electron-dense).
- Scanning EM (SEM): a beam scans a metal-coated surface; gives a three-dimensional-looking image of surfaces such as cilia or red cells.
- Immunogold labelling locates proteins at EM level. Cryo-EM images frozen, unstained samples and can resolve protein structures.
- EM needs a vacuum, so specimens are dead and processing can create artefacts.

Clinical relevance: renal biopsies are routinely examined by light microscopy, immunofluorescence and EM to classify glomerular disease; frozen sections guide surgical margins.

Exam tips: be ready to explain basophilia and eosinophilia in terms of charge, to state resolution limits with the reason, and to choose the right technique for a given question.

All organs are built from four basic tissues: epithelium, connective tissue, muscle and nervous tissue. The syllabus focuses on epithelia, connective and skeletal tissues, and skin.

Epithelia
- Sheets of tightly joined cells resting on a basement membrane, avascular, polarised into apical and basolateral surfaces.
- Classified by number of layers (simple, stratified, pseudostratified) and the shape of the surface cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar).
- Examples: simple squamous (alveoli, endothelium, mesothelium); simple cuboidal (renal tubules, thyroid follicles); simple columnar (stomach; small intestine, with microvilli); pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells (trachea and bronchi); stratified squamous keratinised (epidermis); stratified squamous non-keratinised (oesophagus, vagina, mouth); urothelium or transitional epithelium (bladder, ureter), which stretches.
- Cell junctions: tight junctions (claudins and occludin) seal the paracellular pathway; adherens junctions (cadherins, linked to actin); desmosomes (cadherins, linked to keratin intermediate filaments) give mechanical strength; gap junctions (connexins) allow passage of ions and small molecules; hemidesmosomes (integrins) anchor cells to the basement membrane.
- Basement membrane: basal lamina (type IV collagen, laminin) plus reticular lamina.
- Glands: exocrine (secrete via ducts) or endocrine (into blood). Exocrine secretion may be merocrine (exocytosis, most glands), apocrine (loss of apical cytoplasm, e.g. mammary lipid) or holocrine (whole cell, sebaceous glands).

Connective tissue
- Cells (fibroblasts, adipocytes, macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells) in an extracellular matrix of fibres and ground substance.
- Collagen types: I (tendon, bone, dermis), II (hyaline cartilage), III (reticular fibres in lymphoid organs, liver, early scars), IV (basement membranes, non-fibrillar).
- Elastic fibres: elastin around a fibrillin scaffold (fibrillin is defective in Marfan syndrome).
- Ground substance: glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans that bind water.
- Loose (areolar) vs dense; dense regular (tendons, ligaments, parallel fibres) vs dense irregular (dermis, organ capsules).
- Adipose tissue: white (single large droplet, energy store) and brown (many droplets, mitochondria with UCP1 for heat production; prominent in neonates).

Cartilage
- Avascular; chondrocytes sit in lacunae; nutrition by diffusion, so repair is poor.
- Hyaline (articular surfaces, costal cartilage, trachea, growth plates), elastic (external ear, epiglottis), fibrocartilage (intervertebral disc annulus, menisci, pubic symphysis).

Bone
- Matrix of type I collagen mineralised with hydroxyapatite.
- Cells: osteoblasts make osteoid; osteocytes, trapped in lacunae, communicate via canaliculi and sense load; osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells of the monocyte–macrophage lineage that resorb bone.
- Compact bone is organised into osteons: concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal, linked by perforating (Volkmann's) canals. Spongy (trabecular) bone forms a lattice containing marrow.
- Ossification: intramembranous (flat bones of the skull vault) or endochondral via a cartilage model (long bones; growth plates allow lengthening until fusion after puberty).

Skin
- Epidermis (keratinised stratified squamous) layers from deep to superficial: stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only) and corneum.
- Cells: keratinocytes, melanocytes (neural crest origin, pass melanin to keratinocytes), Langerhans cells (antigen-presenting), Merkel cells (touch).
- Dermis: papillary (loose) and reticular (dense irregular) layers with vessels, nerves and appendages (hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands). Hypodermis below is mostly fat.

Muscle in brief
- Skeletal: long multinucleate striated fibres with peripheral nuclei.
- Cardiac: branched striated cells with one or two central nuclei joined by intercalated discs (desmosomes plus gap junctions).
- Smooth: spindle-shaped, central nucleus, no striations.

Exam tips: always pair an epithelium type with a location and a functional reason; for bone and cartilage, link structure (vascularity, matrix) to repair and loading.

notes.h: Peripheral nervous system tissues, divisions and muscle innervation
notes.body:
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) links the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body. You need its microscopic structure, its somatic and autonomic divisions, and how muscles are innervated.

Tissues of the PNS
- Peripheral nerves are bundles of axons with supporting Schwann cells. A myelinating Schwann cell wraps one internode of a single axon; non-myelinating Schwann cells enclose several small axons (Remak bundles). In the CNS, oligodendrocytes myelinate many axons.
- Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between myelin segments where voltage-gated sodium channels cluster, giving fast saltatory conduction.
- Connective tissue sheaths: endoneurium around each fibre, perineurium around each fascicle (forms a blood–nerve barrier), epineurium around the whole nerve.
- Ganglia: dorsal root ganglia contain pseudounipolar sensory neurons surrounded by satellite cells, with no synapses; autonomic ganglia contain multipolar neurons where pre- and postganglionic neurons synapse.
- Fibre types: large myelinated A-alpha (motor to skeletal muscle, proprioception), A-beta (touch), thin myelinated A-delta (sharp pain, cold), B (preganglionic autonomic), unmyelinated C fibres (dull pain, temperature, postganglionic autonomic). Bigger and myelinated means faster.

Spinal nerves
- 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.
- Dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots join to form a spinal nerve, which splits into dorsal and ventral rami; ventral rami form the cervical, brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.
- A dermatome is the skin area supplied by one spinal nerve; a myotome is the muscle group supplied by one segment.

Autonomic nervous system: two-neuron chain
- Sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1–L2): preganglionic cell bodies in the lateral horn; short myelinated preganglionic fibres leave via white rami communicantes (T1–L2 only) to synapse in the paravertebral sympathetic chain or prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, mesenteric). Postganglionic fibres return to every spinal nerve via grey rami. The adrenal medulla receives preganglionic fibres directly and acts like a modified ganglion.
- Parasympathetic (craniosacral): cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, and sacral S2–S4 (pelvic splanchnic nerves). Long preganglionic fibres synapse in ganglia close to or within the target organ. The vagus supplies thoracic and abdominal viscera as far as about two-thirds along the transverse colon.
- Transmitters: all preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors. Parasympathetic postganglionic release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. Most sympathetic postganglionic release noradrenaline onto adrenoceptors; sympathetic fibres to sweat glands are cholinergic.
- The enteric nervous system (myenteric and submucosal plexuses) can control the gut independently but is modulated by autonomic input.
- Clinical: interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head causes Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on the same side).

Muscle and innervation
- A motor unit is one alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies. Small units (extraocular muscles) give fine control; large units (gastrocnemius) give power.
- At the neuromuscular junction acetylcholine is released, binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate and is broken down by acetylcholinesterase. In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies against the nicotinic receptor cause fatigable weakness.
- Sensory receptors in muscle: muscle spindles (intrafusal fibres sensing length, with gamma motor neuron supply) and Golgi tendon organs (sensing tension).
- Lower motor neuron lesions give weakness, wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone and reflexes; upper motor neuron lesions give weakness, spasticity and brisk reflexes without early wasting.

Exam tips: draw the sympathetic pathway with white and grey rami; know which receptors and transmitters are at each synapse; be able to contrast a peripheral nerve with a CNS tract.

notes.h: Musculoskeletal anatomy: limbs, joints, spine and imaging
notes.body:
This is a large anatomy block. Learn it as patterns (bones, joints, muscle compartments, nerves, arteries) and attach clinical injuries to each nerve.

Bones
- Upper limb: clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius (lateral) and ulna (medial), 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges.
- Lower limb: hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis), femur, patella, tibia (medial, weight-bearing) and fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.

Joints
- Fibrous (skull sutures), cartilaginous (primary: growth plate; secondary: pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs) and synovial.
- Synovial joints have articular hyaline cartilage, a fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane and synovial fluid.
- Types: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (elbow, interphalangeal), pivot (proximal radioulnar, median atlanto-axial), condyloid (wrist, metacarpophalangeal), saddle (first carpometacarpal), plane (acromioclavicular).
- Stability against mobility: the shoulder is very mobile but relies on the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) and dislocates easily, usually anteriorly. The hip is stable thanks to the deep acetabulum, labrum and strong ligaments (iliofemoral is the strongest).
- Knee: the anterior cruciate ligament stops forward movement of the tibia on the femur; the posterior cruciate stops backward movement. The medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament and is injured more often.

Nerves of the upper limb (brachial plexus, C5–T1: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches)
- Musculocutaneous (C5–C7): elbow flexors in the anterior arm.
- Axillary (C5–C6): deltoid and teres minor; at risk in surgical neck of humerus fracture and shoulder dislocation (numb "regimental badge" area).
- Radial (C5–T1): extensors of elbow, wrist and fingers; at risk in mid-shaft humeral fracture (radial groove) causing wrist drop.
- Median (C6–T1): most forearm flexors and thenar muscles; compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome.
- Ulnar (C8–T1): most intrinsic hand muscles; vulnerable behind the medial epicondyle, causing claw hand.
- Erb's palsy (upper trunk, C5–C6) gives the "waiter's tip" posture; Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1) affects the small hand muscles.

Nerves of the lower limb
- Femoral (L2–L4): quadriceps (knee extension) and skin of anterior thigh.
- Obturator (L2–L4): medial thigh adductors.
- Sciatic (L4–S3): hamstrings and, via its tibial and common fibular branches, all muscles below the knee. The common fibular nerve winds round the fibular neck, where injury causes foot drop.
- Superior gluteal (L4–S1): gluteus medius and minimus. Damage gives a positive Trendelenburg sign: the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg.

Arteries
- Subclavian becomes axillary at the outer border of the first rib, then brachial at the lower border of teres major; the brachial divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa; these form the palmar arches.
- External iliac becomes femoral beneath the inguinal ligament (pulse at the mid-inguinal point), then popliteal through the adductor hiatus, dividing into anterior tibial (continues as dorsalis pedis) and posterior tibial arteries, with the fibular branch.

Spine
- 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar vertebrae, sacrum (5 fused) and coccyx.
- Primary curves (thoracic and sacral kyphoses) are present at birth; secondary curves (cervical and lumbar lordoses) develop as the infant holds up its head and walks.
- Atlas (C1) has no body; axis (C2) has the dens.
- Intervertebral disc: outer annulus fibrosus (fibrocartilage) and inner nucleus pulposus (notochord remnant). Herniation is usually posterolateral; in the lumbar spine it usually compresses the nerve root numbered below the disc (an L4/5 disc affects L5).
- The adult spinal cord ends around L1–L2, so lumbar puncture is done at L3/4 or L4/5.

Imaging
- Plain X-ray: dense material (bone, metal) absorbs X-rays and looks white; air looks black. Good for fractures.
- CT: cross-sectional X-ray imaging measured in Hounsfield units (water 0, air −1000); good for complex fractures.
- MRI: no ionising radiation; excellent soft-tissue contrast (discs, ligaments, cord). Fat is bright on T1; fluid is bright on T2.
- Ultrasound: real-time, no radiation, good for tendons and effusions.

Exam tips: for nerve injuries give site, mechanism, motor loss, sensory loss and the characteristic deformity; in Part A, small facts (root values, arterial transitions) are common.

notes.h: Thoracic anatomy, respiratory and cardiovascular morphology
notes.body:
Thoracic wall
- 12 pairs of ribs: 1–7 are true (own costal cartilage to the sternum); 8–12 are false: 8–10 join the cartilage above, and 11–12 are floating.
- Sternum: manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The sternal angle (at the 2nd costal cartilage, level of the T4/T5 disc) marks the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum, roughly the tracheal bifurcation, and the start and end of the aortic arch.
- Intercostal muscles: external, internal and innermost. The neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above down) runs in the costal groove under each rib, so needles and chest drains go just above the upper border of the rib below.
- Diaphragm: supplied by the phrenic nerves (C3–C5). Openings: inferior vena cava at T8, oesophagus at T10, aorta at T12.

Pleura and lungs
- Parietal pleura lines the chest wall and is pain-sensitive (intercostal and phrenic nerves); visceral pleura covers the lung. Air in the space between them is a pneumothorax.
- Right lung: three lobes (horizontal and oblique fissures). Left lung: two lobes (oblique fissure), with the lingula and cardiac notch.
- The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually enter it.
- Each lung is divided into bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own segmental bronchus and artery, so segments can be removed surgically.

Airway histology
- Trachea: C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings with trachealis muscle posteriorly; pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and submucosal glands (the mucociliary escalator).
- Bronchi: cartilage plates, smooth muscle, glands.
- Bronchioles: no cartilage or glands; relatively more smooth muscle; epithelium becomes simple columnar to cuboidal with club cells.
- Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli: gas exchange.
- Alveoli: type I pneumocytes (thin, cover most of the surface, gas exchange) and type II pneumocytes (secrete surfactant and act as progenitors), plus alveolar macrophages. The blood–air barrier is type I cell, fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium.
- Clinical: babies born very prematurely may lack surfactant, causing respiratory distress.

Heart
- Lies in the middle mediastinum within the fibrous and serous pericardium.
- Right atrium receives the venae cavae and coronary sinus; right ventricle pumps to the pulmonary trunk through the pulmonary valve; left atrium receives pulmonary veins; left ventricle (thickest wall) pumps through the aortic valve.
- Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) are held by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, which prevent eversion during systole.
- Conducting system: sinoatrial node (wall of right atrium near the superior vena cava) → atrioventricular node (interatrial septum near the coronary sinus opening) → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
- Coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses. The right coronary supplies the right atrium and ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes. The left main divides into the left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) artery, supplying the anterior left ventricle and most of the septum, and the circumflex artery.
- The apex beat is usually in the 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.

Vessel walls
- Three layers: tunica intima (endothelium), media (smooth muscle and elastin) and adventitia.
- Elastic arteries (aorta) damp pulsatile flow; muscular arteries distribute; arterioles control resistance; capillaries may be continuous (muscle, brain), fenestrated (kidney, endocrine glands, gut) or sinusoidal (liver, spleen, marrow); veins have thinner walls and valves.

Exam tips: know surface landmarks and vertebral levels; essays on the lung or heart reward explicit links between structure (thin barrier, valves, conducting tissue) and function.

notes.h: Abdomen, GI tract, liver and pancreas
notes.body:
Abdominal wall and inguinal canal
- Muscles: rectus abdominis (in the rectus sheath) and three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) meeting in the midline at the linea alba.
- The inguinal canal runs from the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (in the external oblique aponeurosis). It carries the spermatic cord in males or the round ligament in females, and the ilioinguinal nerve.
- An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; a direct hernia pushes through the posterior wall medial to them (Hesselbach's triangle).

Peritoneum
- Intraperitoneal organs are suspended by mesenteries (stomach, jejunum, ileum, transverse and sigmoid colon, liver, spleen).
- Retroperitoneal organs include the kidneys, ureters, adrenals, aorta and IVC, most of the duodenum, the pancreas (except the tail), and the ascending and descending colon.
- The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and communicates with the greater sac via the epiploic foramen.

Gut tube: embryological regions and blood supply
- Foregut (oesophagus to the second part of the duodenum, plus liver, gallbladder, pancreas): coeliac trunk (about T12). Pain is referred to the epigastrium.
- Midgut (second part of duodenum to about two-thirds along the transverse colon): superior mesenteric artery (about L1). Pain referred to the umbilical region.
- Hindgut (distal transverse colon to the upper anal canal): inferior mesenteric artery (about L3). Pain referred to the suprapubic region.

Layers of the GI wall
- Mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa (with the submucosal/Meissner's plexus), muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal layers with the myenteric/Auerbach's plexus between), and serosa or adventitia.
- Oesophagus: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium; muscle is skeletal in the upper third and smooth in the lower third.
- Stomach: simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium with gastric pits; parietal cells (acid and intrinsic factor), chief cells (pepsinogen), G cells in the antrum (gastrin). An extra oblique muscle layer helps churning.
- Small intestine: circular folds, villi and microvilli increase surface area; crypts contain stem cells and Paneth cells (antimicrobial peptides). The duodenum has submucosal Brunner's glands (alkaline mucus); the ileum has Peyer's patches.
- Large intestine: no villi; many goblet cells; longitudinal muscle gathered into three taeniae coli.

Liver
- The classic hepatic lobule is hexagonal with a central vein and portal triads (branches of the hepatic artery and portal vein, plus a bile duct) at the corners.
- Hepatocytes form plates separated by sinusoids lined by fenestrated endothelium; the space of Disse lies between; Kupffer cells (macrophages) sit in sinusoids; stellate cells store vitamin A and drive fibrosis when activated.
- Dual blood supply: the portal vein supplies most of the blood flow; the hepatic artery the remainder, rich in oxygen.
- In the acinus model, zone 1 (periportal) receives the best oxygenated blood and zone 3 (around the central vein) is most vulnerable to hypoxia.
- Bile flows opposite to blood, from canaliculi to bile ducts. The common hepatic and cystic ducts form the common bile duct, which joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, opening at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.
- Clinical: in portal hypertension, portosystemic anastomoses enlarge, for example oesophageal varices.

Pancreas
- Head in the C-loop of the duodenum, then neck, body and tail (reaching the splenic hilum).
- Exocrine acini secrete enzymes stored as zymogen granules; duct cells secrete bicarbonate.
- Endocrine islets of Langerhans: beta cells (insulin, the majority), alpha cells (glucagon), delta cells (somatostatin).

Exam tips: tie organ blood supply and referred pain to embryology; for histology questions, name the layer and cell, then its product.

Kidneys
- Retroperitoneal, roughly T12–L3, with the right kidney slightly lower because of the liver.
- At the hilum, structures from front to back are renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis.
- Cortex and medulla (renal pyramids), papillae draining into minor and major calyces and the renal pelvis.
- Blood path: renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.

The nephron
- Renal corpuscle: glomerular capillaries in Bowman's capsule.
- Filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms (nephrin).
- Proximal convoluted tubule: cuboidal cells with a brush border and many mitochondria; reabsorbs most of the filtrate.
- Loop of Henle: thin limbs lined by simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb of cuboidal cells.
- Distal convoluted tubule, then collecting ducts with principal and intercalated cells.
- Juxtaglomerular apparatus: macula densa cells in the distal tubule, renin-secreting juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole, and extraglomerular mesangial cells.

Ureters, bladder and urethra
- Ureters are muscular tubes lined by urothelium; stones tend to lodge at three narrowings: the pelviureteric junction, where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and the vesicoureteric junction.
- In the female pelvis the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery, which matters in hysterectomy.
- Bladder: detrusor smooth muscle contracts under parasympathetic control (S2–S4); the trigone is a smooth triangle between the ureteric openings and internal urethral orifice. The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve.
- The female urethra is much shorter than the male urethra (prostatic, membranous and spongy parts), one reason urinary infection is more common in women.

Male reproductive system
- Testis: seminiferous tubules containing spermatogenic cells supported by Sertoli cells, whose tight junctions form the blood–testis barrier. Leydig cells in the interstitium produce testosterone under LH. FSH acts on Sertoli cells.
- Sperm mature in the epididymis (pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia) and travel in the thick-walled vas deferens through the inguinal canal to join the seminal vesicle duct, forming the ejaculatory duct in the prostate.
- Accessory glands: seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands.
- The testis develops near the kidney and descends, so the testicular artery arises from the aorta, the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein (the right into the IVC), and testicular lymph drains to para-aortic nodes (whereas scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes).

Female reproductive system
- Ovary: cortex with follicles at stages from primordial to primary, secondary and mature (Graafian), with granulosa and theca cells; after ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone.
- Uterine tube: infundibulum with fimbriae, ampulla (usual site of fertilisation) and isthmus; ciliated and secretory simple columnar epithelium.
- Uterus: endometrium (functional layer shed at menstruation, basal layer regenerates it), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium.
- Cervix: endocervix with mucus-secreting columnar epithelium, ectocervix with stratified squamous epithelium. The transformation zone between them is where most cervical neoplasia arises (associated with high-risk HPV) and is the target of screening.
- Vagina: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
- Blood supply: ovarian artery from the aorta; uterine artery from the internal iliac.

Exam tips: be able to draw and label a nephron and a seminiferous tubule; link embryological descent of the testis to its blood and lymph supply.

Principles
- Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood to distant targets.
- Peptide and protein hormones (insulin, ADH) are water-soluble, stored in granules and act on cell-surface receptors.
- Steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids) are made from cholesterol on demand, are lipid-soluble, travel bound to proteins and act on intracellular receptors that alter gene transcription. Steroid-secreting cells have abundant smooth ER, mitochondria with tubular cristae and lipid droplets.
- Amines: catecholamines behave like peptides; thyroid hormones act on nuclear receptors like steroids.
- Most axes are controlled by negative feedback.

Pituitary
- Sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum; the optic chiasm lies just above it, so an enlarging tumour classically causes bitemporal hemianopia.
- Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) develops from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm). Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones reach it through the hypophyseal portal system. It secretes GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH.
- Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is a downgrowth of the diencephalon. It stores and releases ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin, made by neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and carried down their axons.

Thyroid and parathyroids
- Two lobes joined by an isthmus over about the 2nd–4th tracheal rings; descends in development from the foramen caecum of the tongue along the thyroglossal duct.
- Follicles of cuboidal epithelium store colloid (thyroglobulin), from which T4 and T3 are made using iodine. Parafollicular C cells (reach the thyroid via the ultimopharyngeal body; classically taught as neural crest-derived, though lineage-tracing studies point to an endodermal origin) secrete calcitonin.
- Blood supply: superior thyroid artery (from the external carotid) and inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk). The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the inferior thyroid artery and can be damaged in thyroid surgery, causing hoarseness.
- Usually four parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid; chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH).

Calcium and bone
- PTH raises plasma calcium by increasing bone resorption (indirectly via osteoblasts signalling to osteoclasts through RANKL), increasing renal calcium reabsorption, increasing phosphate excretion and stimulating renal 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D.
- Vitamin D: made in skin with UV light (cholecalciferol), hydroxylated in the liver (25-hydroxy) and kidney (1,25-dihydroxy, calcitriol), which increases intestinal calcium absorption.
- Calcitonin lowers plasma calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts but has a minor role in human calcium balance.

Adrenal gland
- Cortex (mesoderm) has three zones: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol) and reticularis (adrenal androgens).
- Medulla (neural crest) has chromaffin cells secreting mainly adrenaline plus noradrenaline, stimulated directly by preganglionic sympathetic fibres.
- Three arteries (from the inferior phrenic, aorta and renal artery) but one vein each side: right to the IVC, left to the left renal vein.

Endocrine pancreas and gut hormones
- Islets of Langerhans: beta cells (insulin, lowers blood glucose), alpha cells (glucagon, raises it), delta cells (somatostatin). Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells.
- Gut endocrine cells are scattered in the epithelium: gastrin (G cells, gastric antrum; stimulates acid), secretin (S cells, duodenum; stimulates bicarbonate secretion from pancreatic ducts), cholecystokinin (I cells, duodenum and jejunum; gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme release), and incretins GIP and GLP-1, which enhance insulin release after a meal.

Exam tips: for each gland know embryological origin, microscopic zones or cell types, products and one clinical correlation; the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the pituitary–chiasm relation come up often.

Embryology explains adult anatomy: blood supply, nerve supply and congenital anomalies all follow from how structures form.

Weeks 1–2
- Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Cleavage produces a morula, then a blastocyst with an inner cell mass (forms the embryo) and trophoblast (forms the placenta).
- Implantation begins at about the end of the first week, usually in the posterior wall of the uterine body. Implantation elsewhere (most often the uterine tube) is an ectopic pregnancy.
- In week 2 the inner cell mass becomes a bilaminar disc of epiblast and hypoblast, with the amniotic cavity and yolk sac. The trophoblast splits into cytotrophoblast and invasive syncytiotrophoblast, which secretes hCG (the basis of pregnancy tests).

Week 3: gastrulation and the body plan
- The primitive streak appears; epiblast cells migrate through it to form the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
- The notochord forms in the midline and induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate; its remnant is the nucleus pulposus.
- Mesoderm divides into paraxial mesoderm (somites), intermediate mesoderm (urogenital system) and lateral plate mesoderm (somatic layer for body wall and limbs; splanchnic layer for gut wall and heart).
- Somites split into sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle) and dermatome (dermis of the back). Segmental innervation of somite derivatives explains dermatomes.

Neurulation and neural crest
- The neural plate folds into a neural tube, which closes during the fourth week; failure gives neural tube defects such as spina bifida (caudal) or anencephaly (cranial). Maternal folic acid before and in early pregnancy reduces the risk.
- Neural crest cells migrate widely to form dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, much of the skull and face, and part of the outflow tract septum of the heart.

Germ-layer derivatives (main examples)
- Ectoderm: epidermis, nervous system, neural crest, lens, tooth enamel.
- Mesoderm: muscle, bone and connective tissue, heart and vessels, blood, kidneys and gonads, adrenal cortex.
- Endoderm: epithelial lining of the gut and respiratory tract, liver and pancreas parenchyma, thyroid follicular cells, most of the bladder epithelium.

Week 4: folding and organogenesis
- Head-to-tail and lateral folding turn the flat disc into a cylinder, enclosing the gut tube and bringing the heart into the chest.
- Weeks 3–8 are the embryonic period, when organs form and teratogens do most harm; the fetal period from week 9 is mainly growth.

Systems
- Heart: paired tubes fuse into one heart tube, which begins beating early in week 4, loops to the right and is divided by septa. Fetal shunts are the foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus (becomes ligamentum arteriosum) and ductus venosus.
- Limbs: limb buds appear in week 4. The apical ectodermal ridge (FGFs) drives outgrowth; the zone of polarising activity (Sonic hedgehog) sets the thumb-to-little-finger axis; apoptosis separates the digits (failure causes syndactyly).
- Gut: the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord around week 6, rotates 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns around week 10. Errors cause malrotation or omphalocele.
- Urinary: pronephros and mesonephros are transient; the definitive kidney (metanephros) forms from the ureteric bud (collecting system) and metanephric mesenchyme (nephrons), then ascends from the pelvis.
- Genital: SRY on the Y chromosome directs testis formation. Sertoli cells make anti-Müllerian hormone, causing the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts to regress; Leydig cell testosterone keeps the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts, which form the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles; dihydrotestosterone masculinises the external genitalia. Without these signals the Müllerian ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina.
- Head and neck: pharyngeal arches each have a nerve: first (mandibular, trigeminal), second (facial), third (glossopharyngeal), fourth and sixth (vagus).

Exam tips: link each anomaly to the failed step; in essays, explain adult arrangements (gut blood supply, testicular drainage, recurrent laryngeal nerve course) through development.

notes.h: Blood: haematopoiesis, blood cells, haemostasis and plasma proteins
notes.body:
Composition
- Blood is plasma (around 55% of volume) and cells (around 45%; the haematocrit, mostly red cells).
- Plasma proteins, mostly made by the liver: albumin (the most abundant; maintains oncotic pressure and carries hormones, bilirubin and drugs), globulins (including immunoglobulins made by plasma cells) and fibrinogen and other clotting factors. Serum is plasma without clotting factors.
- Low albumin, for example in liver disease or nephrotic syndrome, reduces oncotic pressure and causes oedema.

Haematopoiesis
- Sites change through life: the yolk sac early in the embryo, then the liver (the main fetal site for much of gestation) and spleen, then bone marrow, which takes over before birth.
- In adults, active red marrow is in the axial skeleton (vertebrae, ribs, sternum, skull, pelvis) and proximal ends of the femur and humerus.
- A multipotent haematopoietic stem cell gives a common myeloid progenitor (red cells, platelets via megakaryocytes, granulocytes, monocytes) and a common lymphoid progenitor (B cells, T cells, NK cells).
- Growth factors: erythropoietin, mainly from the kidney in response to hypoxia, drives red cell production; thrombopoietin (mainly liver) drives platelet production; colony-stimulating factors drive white cell production.

Red blood cells
- Biconcave anucleate discs about 7–8 µm across, giving a high surface area for gas exchange and flexibility to squeeze through capillaries.
- No mitochondria, so they rely on glycolysis; they live about 120 days and are removed mainly by macrophages in the spleen.
- Adult haemoglobin (HbA) has two alpha and two beta chains; fetal haemoglobin (two alpha, two gamma) has higher oxygen affinity, helping transfer from mother to fetus.
- Young red cells released from marrow are reticulocytes; a raised reticulocyte count indicates increased production (for example after bleeding or haemolysis).
- The membrane skeleton (spectrin and associated proteins) keeps the shape; defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.
- Haem is broken down to bilirubin, which the liver conjugates and excretes in bile.

White blood cells
- Neutrophils: the most numerous; multilobed nucleus; phagocytose bacteria in acute inflammation.
- Eosinophils: bilobed nucleus with red granules; parasites and allergy.
- Basophils: the rarest; dark granules containing histamine.
- Monocytes: the largest; kidney-shaped nucleus; enter tissues to become macrophages.
- Lymphocytes: small round nucleus with scant cytoplasm; B cells (antibody), T cells (cell-mediated immunity), NK cells.

Platelets and primary haemostasis
- Platelets are anucleate fragments of megakaryocytes and live about 7–10 days.
- After vessel injury: vasoconstriction, then platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen via von Willebrand factor (binding platelet glycoprotein Ib), activation with shape change and release of ADP and thromboxane A2, then aggregation as glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen bridges between platelets. The result is a platelet plug.
- Secondary haemostasis (the coagulation cascade) generates thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin to stabilise the plug.
- Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2 production for the life of the platelet.

Exam tips: be able to identify each blood cell on a smear and state its function; for haemostasis, describe the sequence adhesion → activation → aggregation with the receptor names.

Lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification (hepatocytes) and calcium storage (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle).

Keratins (cytokeratins). Vimentin = mesenchymal cells, desmin = muscle, neurofilaments = neurons, lamins = nuclear envelope.

Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another, e.g. squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium in smokers, columnar metaplasia in Barrett's oesophagus.
Hypertrophy = increase in cell size (LV in hypertension); hyperplasia = increase in cell number (endometrium, prostate).
Disordered growth with nuclear atypia, increased mitoses and loss of maturation; pre-malignant and confined above the basement membrane.

Tumour suppressor genes need both alleles inactivated; in familial retinoblastoma one mutant RB1 allele is inherited, so only one further hit is needed.

Single layer of cells all touching the basement membrane but with nuclei at different heights; with goblet cells; lines trachea and bronchi.
Transitional stratified epithelium with dome-shaped umbrella cells that flatten on stretching; lines renal pelvis, ureters and bladder.

Hyaline (articular, costal, trachea), elastic (ear, epiglottis), fibrocartilage (intervertebral disc, menisci, pubic symphysis).
Structural unit of compact bone: concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal with osteocytes in lacunae linked by canaliculi.
Whole cell disintegrates to form the secretion, e.g. sebaceous glands.
Connective tissue sheath around each nerve fascicle; its cells form a diffusion barrier (blood–nerve barrier).
Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one peripheral axon; an oligodendrocyte myelinates internodes of many CNS axons.
Thoracolumbar, T1–L2; preganglionic cell bodies in the lateral horn; short preganglionic, long postganglionic fibres.
White: myelinated preganglionic fibres entering the sympathetic chain (T1–L2 only). Grey: unmyelinated postganglionic fibres returning to all spinal nerves.
Craniosacral: CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4; long preganglionic fibres to ganglia near or in the target organ.
Sympathetic postganglionic fibres to most sweat glands release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
One alpha motor neuron and all the skeletal muscle fibres it innervates.
Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on the same side due to interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head and neck.
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis (SITS); hold the humeral head in the glenoid.
Surgical neck fracture or shoulder dislocation; weak deltoid (abduction) and teres minor; numb skin over lower deltoid (regimental badge area).

cards.f: Radial nerve in mid-shaft humeral fracture
cards.b: Damaged in the radial groove: wrist drop from paralysis of wrist and finger extensors; triceps usually spared.
At the neck of the fibula; foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion; sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot.
Pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg; weak gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve).
Axillary becomes brachial at the inferior border of teres major.

cards.b: Around L1–L2; lumbar puncture is performed at L3/4 or L4/5.
Posterolateral herniation usually compresses the root numbered below the disc, e.g. L4/5 disc affects L5.
Junction of manubrium and body at 2nd costal cartilage, level of T4/T5 disc; divides superior/inferior mediastinum, near tracheal bifurcation.
IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.
Vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior in the costal groove; insert needles just above the rib below.
Cuboidal alveolar cell that secretes surfactant (lowers surface tension) and can divide to replace type I cells.

cards.f: Why foreign bodies enter the right main bronchus
cards.b: It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
Bronchioles lack cartilage and submucosal glands and have relatively more smooth muscle; bronchi have cartilage plates and glands.
Interatrial septum near the opening of the coronary sinus (triangle of Koch).
Anterior left ventricle, anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum and the apex.
Foregut: coeliac trunk; midgut: superior mesenteric artery; hindgut: inferior mesenteric artery.
Indirect: via deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels. Direct: through posterior wall medial to them (Hesselbach's triangle).
Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor (needed for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum).
Submucosal glands of the duodenum secreting alkaline mucus to protect against gastric acid.
Cells at the base of small-intestinal crypts secreting antimicrobial peptides (e.g. defensins) and lysozyme.
Branch of hepatic artery, branch of portal vein and bile duct (with lymphatics) at the corners of a hepatic lobule.

cards.b: Zone 3 (centrilobular, around the central vein), furthest from the oxygen-rich portal inflow.
Kidneys, ureters, adrenals, aorta, IVC, most of the duodenum, pancreas (not tail), ascending and descending colon, rectum (in part).
Fenestrated capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms.
Macula densa (distal tubule), renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cells (afferent arteriole) and extraglomerular mesangial cells.
Pelviureteric junction, crossing of the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, vesicoureteric junction.
Cuboidal cells with a tall brush border (microvilli) and many basal mitochondria; eosinophilic cytoplasm.
Sertoli: in seminiferous tubules, support spermatogenesis, blood–testis barrier, respond to FSH. Leydig: interstitial, make testosterone under LH.
The left renal vein (the right drains directly into the IVC).
Para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, reflecting embryological origin near the kidney; scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
Junction between endocervical columnar and ectocervical squamous epithelium; site of most cervical neoplasia.

cards.f: Origin of the anterior vs posterior pituitary
cards.b: Anterior: Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm). Posterior: downgrowth of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm).

cards.f: Hormones released by the posterior pituitary
cards.b: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin, synthesised in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.
Glomerulosa: aldosterone; fasciculata: cortisol; reticularis: androgens (outside to inside).
C cells, reaching the thyroid via the ultimopharyngeal body (classically neural crest-derived); secrete calcitonin.

Nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.
Sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle), dermatome (dermis).
Dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, craniofacial skeleton, cardiac outflow septum.
