questions.q: Which organelle is most prominent in a plasma cell actively secreting antibody?
questions.why: Antibodies are secreted proteins made on ribosomes attached to rough ER, which is why plasma cells have basophilic cytoplasm. Smooth ER makes lipids and steroids, peroxisomes oxidise fatty acids and lysosomes digest material; none synthesises secretory protein.

questions.q: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
questions.why: Sister chromatids separate in anaphase once cohesin is cleaved. In prophase chromosomes condense, in metaphase they align at the equator, and in telophase nuclear envelopes re-form around the separated sets.

questions.q: Describe the structure and functions of the three main components of the cytoskeleton, giving one example of each in a named cell or tissue.
markScheme: Microfilaments: actin, about 7 nm; shape, motility, microvilli cores, muscle contraction (e.g. enterocyte microvilli, sarcomere thin filaments)
Intermediate filaments: about 10 nm, rope-like, tensile strength; tissue specific (keratin in epidermis, desmin in muscle, lamins in nucleus)
Microtubules: tubulin dimers, about 25 nm, polar with plus and minus ends, organised by the centrosome
Microtubule functions: transport via kinesin and dynein, mitotic spindle, cilia and flagella (9+2 axoneme, e.g. respiratory epithelium)
Linked to a clinical or functional example (e.g. microtubule-targeting drugs, keratin staining in tumour diagnosis)
questions.modelAnswer: The cytoskeleton has three filament systems. Actin microfilaments (about 7 nm) are polymers of actin that give cells shape, form the core of microvilli in enterocytes and make up the thin filaments of the sarcomere. Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm) are stable, rope-like polymers that resist tension; their type is tissue specific, such as keratins in the epidermis, which anchor at desmosomes, desmin in muscle and lamins lining the nucleus. Microtubules (about 25 nm) are hollow polymers of alpha and beta tubulin organised from the centrosome with polarity; kinesin and dynein carry cargo along them (for example axonal transport in neurons), they form the mitotic spindle, and the 9+2 axoneme of motile cilia in respiratory epithelium. Drugs that disrupt microtubules arrest cells in mitosis.

questions.q: In a long-term smoker, the bronchial epithelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium. This is best described as:
questions.why: Replacement of one differentiated epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar) by another (stratified squamous) is metaplasia. Hyperplasia is more cells of the same type, dysplasia is disordered pre-malignant growth, and anaplasia is lack of differentiation in malignant tumours.

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of apoptosis rather than necrosis?
options: Formation of apoptotic bodies without inflammation
Release of contents provoking acute inflammation
questions.why: Apoptosis shrinks the cell and packages it into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that macrophages remove quietly. Swelling, membrane rupture and inflammation are features of necrosis.

questions.q: Distinguish between hyperplasia, hypertrophy, metaplasia and dysplasia, giving one example of each.
markScheme: Hyperplasia: increased number of cells, e.g. endometrium or benign prostatic hyperplasia
Hypertrophy: increased cell size without division, e.g. left ventricle in hypertension, skeletal muscle in training
Metaplasia: reversible change of one differentiated type to another, e.g. Barrett's oesophagus or bronchial squamous metaplasia
Dysplasia: disordered growth with atypia, pre-malignant, basement membrane intact, e.g. cervical intraepithelial neoplasia
Notes that permanent cells can only respond by hypertrophy, or that metaplasia can progress to dysplasia
questions.modelAnswer: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue and occurs only in cells that can divide, for example the endometrium under oestrogen or the prostate in benign prostatic hyperplasia. Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size without division; it is the only growth response of permanent cells, as in the left ventricle in chronic hypertension. Metaplasia is a reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another better able to cope with a stress, such as columnar glandular epithelium replacing squamous epithelium in the lower oesophagus in Barrett's oesophagus. Dysplasia is disordered growth with nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism and loss of normal maturation, still confined by the basement membrane; cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is an example. Metaplastic epithelium can become dysplastic and then malignant.

questions.q: The nucleus stains blue-purple with haematoxylin mainly because:
options: It contains basic histone proteins only
Its nucleic acids are acidic and bind the basic dye
questions.why: Haematoxylin behaves as a basic dye and binds acidic phosphate groups in DNA and RNA. Histones are basic and would not bind a basic dye; lipid is removed in processing; glycogen is shown by PAS, not haematoxylin.

questions.q: Which technique would best show the arrangement of microvilli on the surface of an enterocyte in three dimensions?
questions.why: SEM images surfaces at high resolution with a three-dimensional appearance. Individual microvilli are below the resolution of light microscopy, where they appear only as a brush border; phase contrast and polarised light also cannot resolve them.

questions.q: Explain why a transmission electron microscope can resolve ribosomes whereas a light microscope cannot, and outline two steps of specimen preparation specific to TEM.
markScheme: Resolution is limited by wavelength (d ≈ λ/2NA); light limit about 0.2 µm
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength, giving resolution around 1 nm or better for biological samples; ribosomes are about 20–30 nm
Glutaraldehyde fixation with osmium tetroxide post-fixation (stains/stabilises lipid)
Resin embedding, ultrathin sectioning and heavy-metal contrast (uranyl acetate, lead citrate)
questions.modelAnswer: Resolution depends on wavelength: for light d ≈ λ/2NA, which is about 0.2 µm at best. Ribosomes are only about 20–30 nm across, so they cannot be resolved with light. Accelerated electrons have a wavelength many orders of magnitude shorter, so TEM can resolve structures around a nanometre in biological specimens. For TEM, tissue is fixed in glutaraldehyde and post-fixed in osmium tetroxide, which preserves membranes and adds contrast to lipids. It is then embedded in hard resin, cut into ultrathin sections tens of nanometres thick, and stained with heavy metals such as uranyl acetate and lead citrate so that structures scatter electrons and appear electron-dense.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the lumen of the oesophagus?
questions.why: The oesophagus needs abrasion resistance but stays moist, so it has non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium. Simple columnar lines the stomach and intestine; keratinised epithelium is the epidermis; pseudostratified ciliated epithelium lines the airways.

questions.q: Which junction allows direct passage of ions between adjacent cardiac muscle cells?
questions.why: Gap junctions made of connexins form channels for ions, allowing electrical coupling in the intercalated discs. Desmosomes provide mechanical attachment, tight junctions seal the paracellular space, and hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basement membrane.

questions.q: Compare hyaline cartilage and compact bone in terms of cells, matrix, blood supply and capacity for repair.
markScheme: Cartilage: chondrocytes in lacunae; matrix of type II collagen and hydrated proteoglycans
Bone: osteoblasts, osteocytes, osteoclasts; type I collagen mineralised with hydroxyapatite, organised into osteons
Cartilage avascular, nourished by diffusion (perichondrium where present); bone highly vascular via Haversian and Volkmann's canals
Cartilage repairs poorly; bone remodels and heals well
Functional link: cartilage resists compression with smooth low-friction surfaces; bone is rigid for support and levers
questions.modelAnswer: Hyaline cartilage contains chondrocytes in lacunae in a matrix rich in type II collagen and water-binding proteoglycans such as aggrecan, which lets it resist compression and provides a smooth articular surface. It is avascular, relying on diffusion from synovial fluid or the perichondrium, so damage heals poorly. Compact bone contains osteoblasts that lay down osteoid, osteocytes that sit in lacunae and sense load via canaliculi, and osteoclasts that resorb bone. Its matrix is type I collagen mineralised with hydroxyapatite, arranged in osteons around Haversian canals carrying vessels, linked by Volkmann's canals. Because it is well vascularised and continually remodelled, bone heals well after fracture.

questions.q: Which receptor type is found on the postganglionic neuron cell bodies of both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia?
questions.why: All preganglionic autonomic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors on postganglionic neurons. Muscarinic receptors are on parasympathetic target organs, and adrenoceptors are on sympathetic targets.

questions.q: The cell bodies of sensory neurons supplying the skin of the forearm are located in:
options: The ventral horn of the spinal cord
The lateral horn of the spinal cord
questions.why: Primary sensory neurons are pseudounipolar cells in the dorsal root ganglia. The ventral horn contains motor neurons, the lateral horn contains sympathetic preganglionic neurons and the sympathetic chain contains postganglionic sympathetic neurons.

questions.q: Describe the pathway taken by sympathetic fibres from the spinal cord to the sweat glands of the skin of the arm, naming the neurotransmitter and receptor at each synapse.
markScheme: Preganglionic cell body in lateral horn (upper thoracic segments, roughly T2–T6 for upper limb)
Leaves via ventral root and spinal nerve, enters chain via white ramus communicans
Ascends in the sympathetic chain to synapse in a cervical or upper thoracic chain ganglion (e.g. stellate/inferior cervical)
Synapse 1: acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors
Postganglionic unmyelinated fibre leaves via grey ramus to join the brachial plexus nerves to the skin
Synapse 2 at sweat gland: acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors (exception to noradrenergic rule)
questions.modelAnswer: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons for the upper limb lie in the lateral horn of the upper thoracic spinal cord (roughly T2–T6). Their myelinated axons leave through the ventral root into the spinal nerve and enter the sympathetic chain via a white ramus communicans. They ascend within the chain and synapse in the cervicothoracic (stellate) or inferior cervical ganglion, where acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors. Unmyelinated postganglionic fibres then leave through grey rami communicantes to join the ventral rami of C5–T1, travel in the brachial plexus branches to the skin, and innervate sweat glands. Unusually, these postganglionic sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine, acting on muscarinic receptors, rather than noradrenaline.

questions.q: A patient cannot extend the wrist after a fracture of the mid-shaft of the humerus. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.why: The radial nerve runs in the radial groove of the humeral shaft and supplies the wrist extensors, so injury causes wrist drop. The median and ulnar nerves supply flexors and intrinsic hand muscles; the musculocutaneous supplies elbow flexors.

questions.q: On a T2-weighted MRI, which of the following appears brightest?
questions.why: Water-rich fluids such as CSF give a high signal on T2-weighted images. Cortical bone, air and tendon have few mobile protons and appear dark on MRI.

questions.q: Describe the factors that contribute to the stability of the hip joint and explain why the shoulder is less stable.
markScheme: Hip: deep acetabulum enclosing most of the femoral head, deepened by the acetabular labrum
Strong capsular ligaments: iliofemoral (strongest), pubofemoral, ischiofemoral; spiral arrangement tightens in extension
Surrounding muscles (gluteals, short lateral rotators) add dynamic stability
Shoulder: shallow glenoid fossa, large humeral head, lax capsule
Shoulder depends mainly on rotator cuff muscles; trade-off of mobility for stability; dislocates more often (usually anteriorly)
questions.modelAnswer: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint in which the deep acetabulum, extended by the fibrocartilaginous labrum, encloses much of the femoral head. Its thick capsule is reinforced by the iliofemoral (strongest), pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments, which spiral and tighten in extension, and powerful surrounding muscles add dynamic stability. The shoulder is also ball-and-socket but its glenoid fossa is shallow relative to the large humeral head and its capsule is lax, so it depends heavily on the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis). This gives a wide range of movement but makes dislocation, usually anterior, much more common.

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm?
questions.why: The oesophageal hiatus is at about T10. The IVC passes at T8 through the central tendon, and the aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament at T12.

questions.q: Which cell type covers most of the alveolar surface and forms part of the blood–air barrier?
questions.why: Type I pneumocytes are very thin squamous cells covering most of the alveolar surface. Type II cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant; club cells are in bronchioles; macrophages are not part of the barrier.

questions.q: Describe the changes in airway wall structure from trachea to alveolus and relate them to function.
markScheme: Trachea: C-shaped hyaline cartilage, posterior trachealis; keeps airway open while allowing oesophageal expansion
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and glands forms the mucociliary escalator
Bronchi: cartilage becomes plates; bronchioles lose cartilage and glands, relatively more smooth muscle (control of airway calibre)
Epithelium thins to simple columnar/cuboidal with club cells in bronchioles
Alveoli: type I (thin barrier for diffusion), type II (surfactant), macrophages
questions.modelAnswer: The trachea is held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, with trachealis muscle posteriorly allowing the oesophagus to expand. It is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and submucosal glands, which trap and clear particles (the mucociliary escalator). In bronchi the cartilage becomes irregular plates. Bronchioles have no cartilage or glands; their walls are dominated by smooth muscle, which controls airway calibre, and the epithelium becomes simple columnar then cuboidal with club cells. In the alveoli the wall is reduced to thin type I pneumocytes over capillaries, giving a very short diffusion distance, with type II cells secreting surfactant to reduce surface tension and macrophages clearing debris.

questions.q: Which artery supplies the jejunum and ileum?
questions.why: The jejunum and ileum are midgut, supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut, the IMA the hindgut, and the left gastric is a coeliac branch to the stomach.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes the duodenum from the jejunum and ileum histologically?
questions.why: Brunner's glands in the submucosa are characteristic of the duodenum. Villi and goblet cells occur throughout the small intestine, and Peyer's patches are characteristic of the ileum.

questions.q: Describe the microscopic structure of the liver lobule and explain how it relates to the flow of blood and bile.
markScheme: Hexagonal lobule with central vein and portal triads (hepatic arteriole, portal venule, bile ductule)
Plates of hepatocytes separated by sinusoids lined by fenestrated endothelium; space of Disse
Blood from portal vein and hepatic artery mixes in sinusoids and flows to central vein, then hepatic veins to IVC
Bile secreted into canaliculi between hepatocytes flows towards portal triads (opposite to blood)
Kupffer cells and stellate cells, or zonation (zone 1 periportal, zone 3 centrilobular)
questions.modelAnswer: The classic lobule is a hexagon of hepatocyte plates radiating from a central vein, with portal triads at its corners containing a branch of the hepatic artery, a branch of the portal vein and a bile ductule. Between the plates run sinusoids lined by fenestrated endothelium, with the space of Disse between endothelium and hepatocytes allowing plasma to reach hepatocyte microvilli. Blood from both portal vein and hepatic artery mixes in the sinusoids and flows towards the central vein, then on to the hepatic veins and IVC. Bile is secreted into canaliculi between adjacent hepatocytes and flows in the opposite direction towards the portal triads. Kupffer cells in the sinusoids remove particles, and periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes receive the most oxygen while centrilobular (zone 3) cells receive the least.

questions.q: A malignant tumour of the testis is most likely to spread first to which lymph nodes?
questions.why: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and descends, taking its lymphatics with it to the para-aortic nodes. Superficial inguinal nodes drain the scrotal skin, not the testis.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the bladder?
questions.why: Urothelium can stretch as the bladder fills, its surface umbrella cells flattening. The other epithelia are not found lining the normal bladder.

questions.q: Outline the structure of the seminiferous tubule and the roles of the cells within and around it.
markScheme: Tubule lined by stratified germinal epithelium on basement membrane, with peritubular myoid cells
Germ cells progress from spermatogonia at the base to spermatocytes, spermatids and spermatozoa towards the lumen
Sertoli cells: support and nourish germ cells, tight junctions form blood–testis barrier, respond to FSH, secrete AMH in development
Leydig cells in interstitium secrete testosterone in response to LH
Myoid cells contract to move sperm; sperm then pass to rete testis and epididymis
questions.modelAnswer: Each seminiferous tubule is lined by a complex stratified epithelium resting on a basement membrane surrounded by contractile peritubular myoid cells. Germ cells mature from spermatogonia near the basement membrane through primary and secondary spermatocytes to spermatids and finally spermatozoa released into the lumen. Tall Sertoli cells span the epithelium; they support and nourish developing germ cells, respond to FSH, and their tight junctions form the blood–testis barrier, protecting meiotic cells from immune attack. In the interstitial tissue between tubules, Leydig cells produce testosterone in response to LH, which is needed for spermatogenesis. Sperm pass via the rete testis to the epididymis to mature.

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex mainly secretes cortisol?
questions.why: The zona fasciculata produces glucocorticoids such as cortisol. The glomerulosa makes aldosterone, the reticularis makes androgens, and the medulla makes catecholamines.

questions.q: Which hormone is released from the duodenum in response to fat and protein and causes gallbladder contraction?
questions.why: Cholecystokinin from I cells contracts the gallbladder and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion. Gastrin stimulates gastric acid, secretin stimulates bicarbonate secretion, and somatostatin is generally inhibitory.

questions.q: Explain how the different embryological origins of the anterior and posterior pituitary relate to how each is controlled by the hypothalamus.
markScheme: Anterior from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm): glandular epithelium, no direct neural connection
Controlled by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones via hypophyseal portal veins
Secretes GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH
Posterior from neural downgrowth of the diencephalon: axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons
ADH and oxytocin made in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, carried down axons and released by nerve impulses (neurosecretion)
questions.modelAnswer: The anterior pituitary develops from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth of oral ectoderm, so it is a true endocrine gland without nerve fibres from the hypothalamus. Hypothalamic neurons instead release releasing and inhibiting hormones into capillaries in the median eminence, and these reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal veins to control secretion of GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH. The posterior pituitary develops as a downgrowth of the diencephalon and remains neural tissue. Its secretions, ADH and oxytocin, are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, transported down axons in the pituitary stalk and released from axon terminals into the circulation in response to action potentials.

questions.q: Which structure is derived from neural crest cells?
questions.why: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are neural crest derivatives. The adrenal cortex is mesodermal, thyroid follicular cells are endodermal, and limb skeletal muscle comes from somitic (paraxial) mesoderm.

questions.q: In a male embryo, the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct is maintained mainly by:
options: hCG acting directly on the duct
questions.why: Testosterone from fetal Leydig cells keeps the Wolffian duct, which forms the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicle. AMH causes Müllerian regression rather than Wolffian maintenance; oestrogen and hCG do not directly maintain the duct.

questions.q: Describe the derivatives of the three regions of intraembryonic mesoderm.
markScheme: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites
Somites: sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle of trunk and limbs), dermatome (dermis of back)
Intermediate mesoderm: urogenital system (kidneys, gonads, genital ducts)
Lateral plate somatic layer: body wall, parietal serous membranes, limb bones and connective tissue
Lateral plate splanchnic layer: gut wall smooth muscle and connective tissue, heart, visceral serosa
questions.modelAnswer: Paraxial mesoderm lies beside the notochord and segments into somites. Each somite forms sclerotome, which makes the vertebrae and ribs; myotome, which makes skeletal muscle of the back, body wall and limbs; and dermatome, which forms the dermis of the back. Intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the urogenital system: the successive kidneys (ending with the metanephros), gonads and genital ducts. Lateral plate mesoderm splits around the intraembryonic coelom. Its somatic layer, with ectoderm, forms the body wall, parietal pleura and peritoneum and the bones and connective tissue of the limbs. Its splanchnic layer, with endoderm, forms the smooth muscle and connective tissue of the gut wall, the visceral serous membranes and the heart.

questions.q: Which white blood cell has a bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules and is increased in parasitic infection?
questions.why: Eosinophils have bilobed nuclei and eosinophilic granules and rise in parasitic infection and allergy. Neutrophils are multilobed with pale granules, basophils have dark blue granules, and monocytes have a kidney-shaped nucleus.

questions.q: Deficiency of von Willebrand factor mainly impairs which step of haemostasis?
questions.why: vWF bridges collagen and platelet GPIb, so deficiency impairs platelet adhesion (primary haemostasis). It also carries factor VIII, but fibrin formation itself is driven by thrombin; fibrinolysis and vasoconstriction are not vWF functions.

questions.q: Relate the structure of the mature red blood cell to its function.
markScheme: Biconcave disc: large surface area to volume ratio for gas diffusion; short diffusion distance
Flexible membrane skeleton (spectrin) lets cells deform through capillaries narrower than their diameter
No nucleus or organelles maximises space for haemoglobin
No mitochondria: relies on glycolysis so does not consume the oxygen it carries; generates 2,3-BPG
Limited lifespan (about 120 days), removed by spleen, because it cannot repair or make proteins
questions.modelAnswer: The red cell is a biconcave disc about 7–8 µm across, giving a large surface area relative to volume and a short diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide. Losing its nucleus and organelles during maturation leaves the cell packed with haemoglobin, maximising oxygen-carrying capacity. Without mitochondria it uses glycolysis for ATP, so it does not consume the oxygen it carries, and a side pathway generates 2,3-BPG that regulates haemoglobin's oxygen affinity. A flexible spectrin-based membrane skeleton lets it deform through capillaries narrower than itself. Because it cannot synthesise new proteins, damage accumulates and it lasts about 120 days before splenic macrophages remove it.

questions.q: Describe the formation and branches of the brachial plexus. Explain, with reference to specific injuries, how damage at different sites produces characteristic patterns of motor and sensory loss in the upper limb.
markScheme: Accurate formation: ventral rami C5–T1; roots, trunks (upper C5–6, middle C7, lower C8–T1), anterior/posterior divisions, lateral/posterior/medial cords named relative to axillary artery
Five terminal branches with root values: musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar
Upper trunk (Erb's) injury: mechanism (shoulder pulled from neck), loss of abduction, lateral rotation, elbow flexion, 'waiter's tip'
Lower trunk (Klumpke's) injury: mechanism (arm pulled upwards), intrinsic hand muscles, claw hand, possible Horner's syndrome via T1
Axillary nerve at surgical neck: deltoid weakness and regimental badge numbness
Radial nerve at mid-shaft humerus: wrist drop, sensory loss over dorsum of first web space
Median nerve at wrist (carpal tunnel) and ulnar nerve at elbow: motor and sensory patterns explained by anatomy
Clear structure, uses principle that deficit reflects muscles and skin distal to the lesion
questions.modelAnswer:
The brachial plexus is formed from the ventral rami of C5 to T1 in the posterior triangle of the neck. The five roots combine into three trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1). Behind the clavicle each trunk splits into anterior and posterior divisions. In the axilla these form three cords named by their relation to the axillary artery: the lateral cord (anterior divisions of upper and middle trunks), the medial cord (anterior division of the lower trunk) and the posterior cord (all three posterior divisions). The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous (C5–C7) from the lateral cord, the axillary (C5–C6) and radial (C5–T1) from the posterior cord, the median (C6–T1) from both lateral and medial cords, and the ulnar (C8–T1) from the medial cord. In general, anterior divisions supply flexor compartments and posterior divisions supply extensors.

Because each nerve supplies particular muscles and skin, the deficit maps to the lesion site. An upper trunk injury (Erb's palsy), caused by forceful widening of the angle between neck and shoulder, for example in a difficult birth or a motorcycle fall, removes C5–C6. Deltoid and supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus (lateral rotation) and biceps and brachialis (elbow flexion and supination) are weakened, so the arm hangs medially rotated and extended with the forearm pronated, the "waiter's tip" posture. Sensation over the lateral arm and forearm is lost.

A lower trunk injury (Klumpke's palsy), from forceful abduction of the arm such as grabbing to stop a fall, affects C8–T1, paralysing the intrinsic hand muscles and producing a claw hand with numbness along the medial forearm and hand. Damage to the T1 root close to the sympathetic chain can add Horner's syndrome.

Injuries to individual nerves give narrower patterns. The axillary nerve, winding round the surgical neck of the humerus, may be injured by fracture there or by shoulder dislocation, weakening deltoid and teres minor and numbing the lower deltoid skin. The radial nerve in the radial groove is vulnerable in mid-shaft fractures, giving wrist drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the first web space; triceps is usually spared because its branches arise higher. The median nerve compressed in the carpal tunnel causes thenar wasting, weakness of thumb abduction and opposition, and tingling in the lateral three and a half digits, while the palm is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum. The ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle causes weakness of most intrinsic hand muscles, clawing of the ring and little fingers and sensory loss over the medial one and a half digits. Overall, deficits always involve structures distal to the lesion, so careful examination localises the injury.

questions.q: Explain how the embryological development of the gut tube accounts for the arterial supply, autonomic innervation and pattern of referred pain of the adult abdominal viscera. Illustrate your answer with one congenital anomaly.
markScheme: Folding in week 4 incorporates the yolk sac endoderm to form foregut, midgut and hindgut, suspended by dorsal mesentery
Each region supplied by its unpaired ventral branch of the aorta: coeliac (foregut), SMA (midgut), IMA (hindgut), with correct boundaries
Organs budding from foregut (liver, pancreas, gallbladder) share coeliac supply
Visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres to spinal segments; pain is poorly localised, midline, referred to dermatomes of those segments (epigastric, umbilical, suprapubic)
Parasympathetic: vagus to foregut and midgut; pelvic splanchnic S2–S4 to hindgut (link to vagal limit near distal transverse colon)
Midgut herniation and 270° anticlockwise rotation around SMA explain position of caecum and duodenojejunal flexure
Congenital anomaly correctly explained, e.g. malrotation with volvulus, omphalocele, Meckel's diverticulum (vitelline duct remnant)
Clinical example of referred pain, e.g. early appendicitis felt periumbilically before localising to right iliac fossa
questions.modelAnswer:
During the fourth week, head-to-tail and lateral folding of the embryo pinches off the dorsal part of the endoderm-lined yolk sac to form the primitive gut tube, suspended from the posterior body wall by a dorsal mesentery. The gut is divided into foregut, midgut and hindgut, and each region is supplied by a single unpaired ventral branch of the abdominal aorta running in its mesentery. The foregut, from the abdominal oesophagus to the second part of the duodenum near the major papilla, is supplied by the coeliac trunk; organs budding from it (liver, gallbladder and pancreas) and the spleen, which develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, share this supply. The midgut, from the second part of the duodenum to about two-thirds along the transverse colon, is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The hindgut, from the distal transverse colon to the upper anal canal, is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery. The junctions between territories are watershed areas joined by anastomoses.

Innervation follows the same plan. Sympathetic fibres reach each region through splanchnic nerves and the prevertebral ganglia at the roots of these arteries (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric ganglia). Parasympathetic supply to foregut and midgut is from the vagus, whose territory ends near the distal transverse colon; the hindgut receives pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4). Visceral pain fibres run back with the sympathetic nerves to the spinal segments that supplied the embryonic region. Because the gut began as a midline structure supplied bilaterally, visceral pain is poorly localised and felt in the midline, referred to the dermatomes of those segments: foregut pain in the epigastrium, midgut pain around the umbilicus and hindgut pain in the suprapubic region. Early appendicitis therefore causes periumbilical pain; only when the inflamed appendix irritates the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum does pain move to the right iliac fossa.

Gut rotation explains the adult positions. Around week 6 the rapidly growing midgut herniates into the umbilical cord, rotating 270° anticlockwise (viewed from the front) around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery, then returns to the abdomen around week 10. As a result the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the left, the caecum descends to the right iliac fossa, and the transverse colon crosses in front of the duodenum.

Errors in this process cause congenital anomalies. In malrotation, incomplete rotation leaves the small bowel mesentery on a narrow base, so the midgut can twist around the superior mesenteric artery (volvulus), cutting off its blood supply and causing bilious vomiting in a neonate, which is a surgical emergency. Failure of the herniated bowel to return gives an omphalocele covered by amnion. Persistence of part of the vitelline duct gives a Meckel's diverticulum on the ileum. In each case the anomaly is a logical consequence of a specific developmental step going wrong.
